newsitem.title: BULGARIA: IMF funds delay to keep Bulgarian economy reeling.
newsitem.headline: IMF funds delay to keep Bulgarian economy reeling.

text.p: High interest rates, a weak lev and soaring inflation will continue to batter Bulgaria's economy after the International Monetary Fund (IMF) again delayed funding due to the slow pace of reform, analysts said on Monday.

Sofia's failure to convince the IMF it was making significant steps towards economic reform has prompted a one-month delay in a crucial $115 million IMF loan payment and prompted speculation about Bulgaria's ability to service its foreign debt.
"The macreconomic parameters will deteriorate, but there is no short-term danger of defaulting," Krassen Stanchev, head of the Institute on Market Economy, told Reuters.

On Saturday, Finance Minister Dimitar Kostov said the IMF had refused to agree the second tranche of a $580 million facility. He said it was important the funding arrived by the end of 1996 as the next big debt payment was due next year.
Coupon payments of around $130 million on some $5 billion worth of Brady Bonds are due at the end of January.

Foreign debt payments due until end-1996 amounting to around $150 million and January's coupon on Bradies can be covered by the central bank foreign exchange reserves, which stood at $575 million in August, a central bank officials said.
World Bank consultant Mariela Nenova said the central bank might dip into its reserves to intervene on the local foreign exchange market to support the weakening lev.

The lev, which firmed last week from 231 to the dollar to 212 on Friday after the central bank hiked its central interest rate to a record 300 percent the previous week, eased on Monday to 217.5 on news of the delayed funding.
Last week many dealers focused on lev investments to profit from the high yields, but on Monday demand rose for dollars seen as the most reliable investment in the region.
Nenova said monthly inflation was expected to remain high at between 15 and 20 percent. Inflation in August stood at 17.1 percent.
"It is unlikely that the central bank will be able to reduce the central interest rate under these circumstances," she said.
The central bank was under pressure to reduce the rate in a bid to boost investment in the crumbling real economy.
"But I suppose the IMF would focus more on actual restructuring changes than macroeconomic targets," said Nenova.
Sofia has overshot its macroeconomic targets, already revised in mid-year. The annual interest rate target of 65 percent and annual inflation of 105 percent have both been breached.
"There is no reason to receive the tranche now, which if not spent immediately on foreign debt payments, will be siphoned through interventions to support the lev," said Nenova.
The government has pledged to close or sell off 64 loss-making state enterprises this month and speed up privatisation by year-end.

But legal tangles, lack of experience in closing enterprises which have operated with various levels of success for decades, and the desire to save production considered viable by the government have delayed closures.
In a desperate attempt to raise cash, the Socialist government plans to privatise up to 20 bigger state firms, hoping to raise around $1 billion.
The country needs around $350 million by the end of the year to cover current expenses, which include fuel and grain supplies, said the Kapital business weekly.
One quarter of Bulgaria's banks have been placed under special supervision with the aim of seeking their insolvency through the courts.

An IMF mission is expected in Sofia by the end of October to evaluate the stabilisation measures and decide on the macroeconomic assumptions for next year's budget framework. It is also expected to complete the first stage of the reform programme review and decide on further funding.
